title: Is your parent still safe living alone in New Jersey?
dek: The warning signs to watch for, how to raise the subject, who can assess your parent, what help at home costs in New Jersey and a step-by-step plan for what comes next.
keyFacts: The ADRC at 1-877-222-3737 connects you to your parent's county office on aging for a free screening.
NJ median home care cost was $38 an hour in 2025 (CareScout).
MLTSS 2026: income up to $2,982 a month and $2,000 in assets for a single applicant.
JACC 2026: for people 60+ with income up to $4,855 a month who are not on Medicaid.
Guardianship in NJ needs statements from two physicians, or a physician and a psychologist.
body:
It often starts with something small. A pile of unopened mail on the kitchen table. A dent in the car nobody mentions. The same story told three times in one phone call. You start to wonder whether Mom or Dad is still safe living alone.

There is no single test that answers that question. There is a sensible way to work through it, though, and New Jersey has more help than most families realize. This guide covers the warning signs, how to raise the subject, how to get a professional assessment, what in-home help costs here, and the next steps if staying home is no longer enough.

What are the warning signs?

Look for patterns, not one bad day. Visit in person if you can, and stay long enough to see a normal routine. Signs that deserve a closer look include:

In the house

  • Spoiled food in the refrigerator, or very little food at all
  • Unpaid bills, late notices or stacks of unopened mail
  • A messier house than usual, or laundry and dishes piling up
  • Burned pots, a stove left on or scorch marks
  • Pill bottles that are too full or too empty for the date
  • Thermostat set very high or very low, especially in a New Jersey winter

In your parent

  • Weight loss, poor hygiene or wearing the same clothes for days
  • Bruises, a new limp or a fall they did not mention
  • Missed appointments, getting lost on familiar routes or new dents on the car
  • Repeating questions, confusion about the day or trouble following a conversation
  • Pulling away from friends, church or the senior center
  • New "friends," unusual purchases or calls asking for money

Falls deserve special attention. The CDC says more than one in four adults 65 and older falls each year, and falling once doubles the chance of falling again. Our fall prevention guide covers what helps.

A sudden change is a medical question first. Call the doctor before you call a moving company.

Sudden confusion can come from an infection, dehydration or a medicine problem, and it may be treatable. If your parent seems very different from a week ago, call the doctor that day.

How do I bring it up without a fight?

Most older adults want to stay in their own home, and they are entitled to make their own choices as long as they are able. Go in ready to listen.

  • Pick a calm time. Not during a holiday dinner, and not right after a scare if you can help it.
  • Start with what you saw. "I noticed the stove was on when I came in" lands better than "You can't take care of yourself."
  • Ask what worries them. Your parent may already be scared about the stairs or the bills and relieved to talk.
  • Talk about staying home safely. For most people, help at home is the goal. Moving is one option among several.
  • Bring siblings in early. Agree on the facts before you agree on a plan.
  • Expect more than one conversation.

Our guide to the first conversation about care has more scripts and tips.

Who can do a professional assessment?

An outside opinion helps when the family cannot agree, or when you live far away. There are three main routes in New Jersey.

The county office on aging and the ADRC

Call the Aging and Disability Resource Connection (ADRC) at 1-877-222-3737. It connects you to the Area Agency on Aging in your parent's county. The state's 2026 Program Guide says these offices give information, screening and options counseling, and can help with applications for programs such as Medicaid. Services they provide or coordinate include friendly visiting, telephone reassurance, home repairs, housekeeping, adult day care, transportation and meals. Home-delivered meals are for people 60 and older who are homebound and cannot make meals for themselves, and the driver checks in at each delivery. See our meals guide.

A geriatric care manager

A private geriatric care manager, usually a licensed social worker or nurse, visits your parent at home and writes a care plan. They can screen home care agencies, go to doctor visits and keep far-away family updated. Medicare does not pay for it. Read when to call a geriatric care manager, or browse care managers on our find care help page.

The doctor

Ask for a visit focused on safety and memory. Medicare's yearly Wellness visit includes a cognitive assessment to look for signs of dementia and a review of current prescriptions. If the provider finds a concern, Medicare covers a separate, more detailed visit. Ask your parent to sign the office's permission form so the doctor can talk with you.

What in-home help is there, and what does it cost in New Jersey?

Help at home ranges from a few hours a week to around the clock. Rates vary by county, by agency and by schedule. For a benchmark, the CareScout Cost of Care Survey 2025 put New Jersey's median costs at:

Type of care (NJ median, 2025)Cost
Home care, non-medical aide$38 an hour
Adult day health care$100 a day
Assisted living, private one-bedroom$8,710 a month
Nursing home, semi-private room$12,775 a month

At $38 an hour, an aide four hours a day, three days a week comes to about $1,980 a month. Before you hire, read our guides to choosing a home care agency in NJ and senior care costs in NJ.

Medicare covers home health care only when a person is homebound and needs part-time skilled care ordered by a doctor. It does not cover ongoing help with bathing, dressing or meals when that is the only care needed. Most aide care is paid privately, by long-term care insurance or through the programs below.

State and Medicaid programs

  • MLTSS. New Jersey's Medicaid long-term care benefit, Managed Long Term Services and Supports, can pay for personal care at home, adult day, respite, meals, home modifications, a personal emergency response system, assisted living and nursing home care. Your parent must need a nursing home level of care and meet the financial rules. In 2026 the income limit is $2,982 a month, with a $2,000 asset limit for a single person and a five-year look-back. Read our MLTSS guide.
  • JACC. Jersey Assistance for Community Caregiving is state-funded for people 60 and older who need a nursing home level of care but are not on Medicaid. In 2026 the income limit is $4,855 a month for one person and countable assets must be $40,000 or less. Services are capped at $1,156 a month plus care management. See our JACC guide.
  • Statewide Respite Care Program. Gives the family caregiver a break. In 2026 a single care recipient may have up to $2,982 a month in income and $40,000 in liquid assets. Our respite guide has details.
  • PACE. An all-in-one program for people 55 and older who need a nursing home level of care, with a day center, medical care and home care. The state has funded PACE in all 21 counties, though some new centers are still being built.

Every one of these starts with the ADRC call.

When is adult day or assisted living the better fit?

Adult day

Adult day is often the missing middle. Your parent spends the day at a center and sleeps at home. New Jersey has two kinds. Adult day health services provide nursing care, at least one full meal, activities, personal care and transportation to and from home. Social day centers are for people who need supervision more than medical care. Funding can include MLTSS, JACC, the Alzheimer's Adult Day Services Program, VA benefits, the Statewide Respite Care Program and private pay. The state's 2026 Program Guide notes that coverage areas follow travel time, not county lines. You can search licensed adult day centers on the NJ Department of Health facility search.

Assisted living

Assisted living may make sense when your parent needs help several times a day, gets lonely at home, or the house itself has become the problem. It includes housing, meals and personal care. Not every residence accepts Medicaid, and some require a period of private pay first, so ask in writing. Compare options in assisted living vs. home care and housing options in NJ.

What if my parent refuses help or can no longer decide?

An adult who understands the risks has the right to make choices you disagree with. Keep talking, offer small steps and stay close.

The best protection is planning while your parent can still decide. A durable power of attorney and an advance directive let a trusted person act if your parent later cannot. See our estate planning guide.

Adult Protective Services

If you believe your parent is being abused, neglected or exploited, or cannot care for themselves and is in danger, contact the Adult Protective Services (APS) office in their county. APS serves adults 18 and older living in the community who cannot protect themselves. A trained social worker meets the person in private, and the information is confidential. Find your county office on the state's APS page or through the ADRC. In an emergency, call 911. Our elder abuse guide explains more.

Guardianship basics

Guardianship is a court process and a last resort. In New Jersey the case is filed with the county Surrogate and heard in Superior Court. The court rules require sworn statements from two physicians, or from one physician and one licensed psychologist, about the person's capacity. The court appoints a lawyer for the parent, proposed guardians go through background screening, and guardians must file periodic reports. Fees vary by county. If no family member can serve, the state's Office of the Public Guardian may be appointed for adults 60 and older, at 609-588-6500. Talk with an elder law attorney first.

What is a good step-by-step plan?

  1. Write down what you see. Dates, falls, missed bills and changes in mood or memory.
  2. Book a doctor visit. Rule out treatable causes, review medicines and ask about memory.
  3. Call the ADRC at 1-877-222-3737. Ask for a screening and a list of county services.
  4. Talk with your parent. Agree on one or two changes to start, such as meals, a weekly aide or a medical alert button.
  5. Make the home safer. Grab bars, railings, lighting and a clear path to the bathroom.
  6. Get the paperwork in place. Power of attorney, advance directive and permission forms for doctors.
  7. Set up a check-in routine. A daily call, a neighbor with a key and a shared family calendar.
  8. Review every few months. If needs grow, revisit adult day, more aide hours, MLTSS or a move.

For Medicare questions along the way, call SHIP at 1-800-792-8820. For local services of any kind, dial 2-1-1. And look after yourself too. Our caregiver burnout guide can help.

faq.q: How do I know if my elderly parent should not live alone?
faq.a: Watch for patterns such as falls, missed medicines, spoiled food, unpaid bills, weight loss, getting lost or a stove left on. One sign alone may be fixable. Several together mean it is time for a doctor visit and a professional assessment.

faq.q: Who can assess whether my parent is safe at home in New Jersey?
faq.a: Call the ADRC at 1-877-222-3737 to reach your county office on aging, which offers screening and options counseling at no cost. A private geriatric care manager can do a detailed home assessment for a fee, and your parent's doctor can check memory and medicines.

faq.q: How much does in-home care cost in New Jersey?
faq.a: The CareScout Cost of Care Survey 2025 put New Jersey's median at $38 an hour for a non-medical home care aide. Adult day health care was $100 a day. Get written quotes, since rates vary by county and schedule.

faq.q: Does Medicare pay for an aide for a parent living alone?
faq.a: Not for ongoing help with bathing, dressing or meals. Medicare covers part-time skilled home health care when a person is homebound and a doctor orders it. NJ programs such as MLTSS and JACC can pay for aide care for people who qualify.

faq.q: What can I do if my parent refuses help?
faq.a: An adult who understands the risks can make their own choices. Keep talking, start with small steps and involve their doctor. If you believe they are being neglected, exploited or are in danger, contact the county Adult Protective Services office.

faq.q: How does guardianship work in New Jersey?
faq.a: It is a court case filed with the county Surrogate and heard in Superior Court. The court needs statements from two physicians, or a physician and a licensed psychologist, and appoints a lawyer for the parent. Talk with an elder law attorney first.

title: Caregiver burnout in NJ: signs, respite and where to get help
dek: Feeling worn down from caring for a parent or spouse? Here are the warning signs, quick ways to lighten the load, and the New Jersey programs that give family caregivers real time off.
keyFacts: Statewide Respite Care Program 2026: care recipient income up to $2,982 a month (single)
Every county has a respite program: call the ADRC at 1-877-222-3737
NJ Family Leave Insurance 2026: 85% of wages, up to $1,119 a week
Alzheimer's Association 24/7 helpline: 1-800-272-3900
In crisis? Call or text 988, any hour
body:
Caregiving rarely starts with a decision. It starts with a ride to the cardiologist, then the pill organizer, then the grocery runs, then the calls at night. A year later you are running a second household and wondering why you feel so flat.

That worn out, running on empty feeling has a name. Caregiver burnout is physical, mental and emotional exhaustion that builds when the work of caring goes on for months with too little rest or help. It is common, and it is fixable. This guide covers the warning signs, quick ways to lighten the load, and the New Jersey programs that can give you real time off.

What does caregiver burnout look like?

Burnout creeps in. Many caregivers are so focused on the person they care for that they miss the signs in themselves. The National Institute on Aging and Mayo Clinic list these common warning signs:

  • Feeling exhausted, overwhelmed or anxious most of the time
  • Snapping at people, or feeling impatient and angry more often
  • Sleeping too little, or too much
  • Losing interest in things you used to enjoy
  • Feeling lonely, sad or hopeless
  • Frequent headaches, pain or other physical problems
  • Skipping your own doctor visits, meals or showers
  • Leaning on alcohol, sleep aids or other drugs to get through

Some situations raise the risk. Mayo Clinic points to caring for a spouse, living with the person, providing constant care, money worries and feeling you had no choice in the role. If two or three of those describe you, plan for help now, before a crisis forces it.

You cannot pour from an empty pitcher. Getting help is part of the care plan.

How can you lighten the load right away?

Big programs take time to set up. These steps can make a difference this week.

  • Write down everything you do. Rides, meals, pills, bills, laundry, calls, overnight checks. A list makes the work visible to you and to the family.
  • Hand out specific jobs. People who say "let me know if you need anything" rarely follow through on their own. Give them one job: Tuesday dinner, the pharmacy run, Sunday afternoon with Dad. The National Institute on Aging suggests letting each helper pick from your list.
  • Use a text if asking is hard. A group text to siblings with three clear asks often works better than a tense phone call.
  • Cut what can wait. Hosting the holiday dinner, a spotless house and every optional appointment can go for a season.
  • Bundle the errands. Ask the pharmacy about refill sync and home delivery. Set up automatic bill pay where you can.
  • Tell your own doctor you are a caregiver. It changes the conversation about your sleep, blood pressure and mood.

If the family has never sat down to divide the work, our guide to the first conversation about care can help you plan it.

What respite help does New Jersey offer?

Respite means someone else takes over for a while so you can rest. New Jersey funds several programs that pay for it, all reached through your county office on aging. The Aging and Disability Resource Connection (ADRC) at 1-877-222-3737 routes you to the right county.

Statewide Respite Care Program

The Statewide Respite Care Program (SRCP) runs in every county. It gives unpaid family caregivers a break, whether that means a few afternoons a week of in-home help, time at an adult day center or a short stay in a facility while you travel or recover from your own surgery. Eligibility is based on the person receiving care, who must be 18 or older, live in the community in New Jersey and have a medical provider certify that they need another person's care.

SRCP limit (2026)SingleMarried
Gross monthly incomeUp to $2,982Up to $5,964 combined
Liquid assetsUp to $40,000Up to $60,000 combined
Cost shareSliding scale, 0% to 25% of service costs

JACC

Jersey Assistance for Community Caregiving (JACC) is for people 60 and older who need nursing home level care and are not on Medicaid. A care manager builds a plan that can include respite, home care, adult day, meals and a personal emergency button. Our JACC guide covers the 2026 limits. A person cannot be in JACC and SRCP at the same time, so the county will help you pick one.

Adult day programs

Adult day centers give you regular weekday hours off while your loved one gets meals, activities and company. Many offer transportation. If dementia is part of the picture, the state's Alzheimer's Adult Day Services Program helps pay for adult day at participating centers, covering 20% to 100% of the cost for up to five days a week. You apply through the center. Ask for current income limits, since the state page still showed 2025 figures in October 2026.

Alzheimer's New Jersey, a statewide nonprofit, also runs a Respite Care and Wellness program. Its website describes a $1,000 reimbursement toward respite care costs. Call 973-586-4300 to ask whether funds are available now.

For a full side by side of these programs, see our caregiver respite guide. To find adult day centers and care managers near you, try our Find care help pages.

Where can New Jersey caregivers find support?

Talking with people who understand can lift a weight that no schedule change will. These are free and open to New Jersey families.

  • Alzheimer's Association New Jersey Chapter. Its helpline at 1-800-272-3900 answers 24 hours a day and can point you to caregiver support groups and free education programs near you.
  • Alzheimer's New Jersey. Professionally staffed helpline at 1-888-280-6055, Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m., with translation in over 200 languages.
  • Stress-Busting Program for Family Caregivers. A nine-week state program with weekly 90-minute sessions in a small group. It is built for people caring for someone with dementia or a chronic illness. Call the Division of Aging Services at 609-564-2617 or the ADRC at 1-877-222-3737 to find a class.
  • Care2Caregivers. A peer support line through Rutgers, answered by trained peer counselors who have been family caregivers themselves: 1-800-424-2494.
  • Well Spouse Association. For husbands, wives and partners who are caregivers: 1-800-838-0879.
  • Your county office on aging. Ask about caregiver programs, training and local support groups. Find yours on our county pages or through the ADRC.

Houses of worship, hospitals and senior centers often host groups as well. If one group does not feel right, try another. Fit matters.

If you care for someone with memory loss, our dementia support guide lists memory cafes and safety programs.

Can you get paid, or take paid time off?

Money stress feeds burnout. Two New Jersey options are worth checking.

Getting paid as a family caregiver

Some family members can be paid through NJ FamilyCare's Personal Preference Program, and veterans may have VA options. Our guide on how to get paid as a family caregiver in NJ walks through each path.

Family Leave Insurance

If you work in New Jersey, Family Leave Insurance (FLI) can partly replace your pay while you care for a family member with a serious physical or mental health condition. Most NJ workers already pay into it through payroll.

Family Leave Insurance (2026)Details
Weekly benefit85% of your average weekly wage, up to $1,119
Continuous leaveUp to 12 weeks in a 12-month period
Intermittent leaveUp to 56 separate days in a 12-month period
Earnings to qualify20 weeks at $310 or more a week, or $15,500 total in your base year

Intermittent leave is often the better fit for caregivers. You can take a day for each chemo session or a week after a hospital discharge. "Family" is broad, covering parents, parents-in-law, spouses, siblings, grandparents, grandchildren, domestic partners, other blood relatives and anyone you consider family.

New Jersey also widened job protection on July 17, 2026. If you receive FLI benefits, your job is now generally protected during that leave even at a small employer, and the NJ Family Leave Act now covers employers with 15 or more workers. Check the details at myleavebenefits.nj.gov/jobprotection.

How to apply: Give your employer notice (15 days for intermittent leave when you can), then file online at myleavebenefits.nj.gov. You can start up to 60 days ahead and have 30 days after leave begins to file. The doctor of the person you care for completes a medical certification using the form ID you give them.

What if you feel you cannot go on?

Caregivers carry a lot of grief, guilt and anger, often all at once. Those feelings are normal. If they turn into hopelessness, or thoughts of hurting yourself or the person you care for, reach out today.

  • 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. Call or text 988, or chat online, any hour. It is free and confidential, and counselors talk with anyone in emotional distress.
  • NJ Hopeline. New Jersey's 24-hour mental health and suicide prevention line: 1-855-654-6735.
  • Emergency. If anyone is in immediate danger, call 911.

For ongoing help, ask your doctor for a counselor referral and check your health plan's mental health benefits.

What does a one-week reset look like?

You do not need a perfect plan. You need a few days of steady progress. Here is a simple week to start.

  1. Day 1, take stock. List every caregiving task and how long it takes. Circle the three that drain you most.
  2. Day 2, make one call. Call the ADRC at 1-877-222-3737 and ask about the Statewide Respite Care Program, JACC and adult day. Have income and savings figures for the person you care for at hand.
  3. Day 3, ask for help. Send siblings or friends one specific request each, with a day and time.
  4. Day 4, book your own appointment. Schedule the checkup, dental cleaning or screening you have been putting off.
  5. Day 5, find your people. Call one helpline or sign up for one support group or Stress-Busting class.
  6. Day 6, take two hours off. Line up a relative, friend or paid aide, and leave the house. A walk, lunch with a friend, a matinee. No errands.
  7. Day 7, plan the next month. Put recurring breaks on the calendar. If you work, look into Family Leave Insurance before you need it.

Repeat what worked. Drop what did not. Small breaks taken often do more than one big vacation you never get to take.

faq.q: What is caregiver burnout?
faq.a: It is physical, mental and emotional exhaustion that builds when someone cares for a loved one for a long time without enough rest or help. Common signs include constant tiredness, poor sleep, irritability, sadness, losing interest in things you enjoy and skipping your own health care.

faq.q: How do I get respite care in New Jersey?
faq.a: Call the Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737. It connects you to your county's Statewide Respite Care Program and other options such as JACC and adult day. In 2026 the respite program serves care recipients with gross income up to $2,982 a month (single) or $5,964 (married) and liquid assets up to $40,000 or $60,000.

faq.q: Can I get paid leave to care for my mother in New Jersey?
faq.a: Yes, if you work in New Jersey and meet the earnings test. Family Leave Insurance pays 85% of your average weekly wage, up to $1,119 a week in 2026, for up to 12 weeks in a row or 56 separate days in a 12-month period. Apply at myleavebenefits.nj.gov.

faq.q: Are there free caregiver support groups in NJ?
faq.a: Yes. The Alzheimer's Association New Jersey Chapter (1-800-272-3900) and Alzheimer's New Jersey (1-888-280-6055) can point you to groups. The state's Stress-Busting Program for Family Caregivers runs nine-week classes; call 609-564-2617. Your county office on aging may also run groups.

faq.q: Who can I call if caregiving feels like too much?
faq.a: Call or text 988, the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, any time for free, confidential support. New Jersey's NJ Hopeline is 1-855-654-6735. If anyone is in immediate danger, call 911.

title: Sundowning in dementia: evening routines and help for NJ families
dek: Late-day confusion and agitation are common in dementia. Here is what tends to set it off, routines that calm evenings, when to call the doctor and where New Jersey families can get support.
keyFacts: Sundowning means confusion or agitation that builds in the late afternoon and evening
Common triggers: fatigue, low light, hunger, pain, noise and infections
Sudden worsening can signal a urinary tract infection: call the doctor
Alzheimer's Association 24/7 helpline: 1-800-272-3900
NJ respite and adult day programs: ADRC 1-877-222-3737
body:
Many families know the pattern. Mom is calm and chatty at lunch. By 4 or 5 o'clock she is pacing, asking to go home even though she is home, or accusing you of hiding her purse. By bedtime everyone is exhausted.

This late-day shift is called sundowning. It is one of the hardest parts of caring for someone with dementia, and one of the most common reasons families reach out for help. The good news is that small changes to the day often ease it. This guide explains what sundowning is, what tends to set it off, routines that help, when to call the doctor and where New Jersey families can get support.

What is sundowning?

Sundowning is increased confusion, restlessness or agitation that starts in the late afternoon or early evening and can last into the night. The Alzheimer's Association calls it a set of symptoms that come with brain changes from dementia. It can affect people with Alzheimer's disease and other types of dementia.

It can look like:

  • Pacing, rummaging or trying to leave the house
  • Anxiety, irritability or sudden anger
  • Confusion about where they are or what time it is
  • Seeing or hearing things that are not there
  • Trouble falling asleep, or waking up upset during the night

The exact cause is not known. Experts think changes in the brain disrupt the body's internal clock, so the person may feel sleepy during the day and wide awake at night.

Sundowning usually has a pattern. Find the pattern and you can often get ahead of it.

What triggers sundowning?

The National Institute on Aging, the Alzheimer's Association and Mayo Clinic list similar triggers. Many are things you can change.

  • Being overtired. A full day of visits, appointments or errands can catch up by late afternoon.
  • Low light and shadows. Dim rooms and long shadows can be misread, which may cause fear or hallucinations.
  • A mixed-up body clock. Long naps and little daylight make nights harder.
  • Hunger, thirst or needing the bathroom. The person may not be able to tell you.
  • Pain, boredom or depression.
  • An unfamiliar place. A hospital stay, a holiday at a relative's house or new furniture can unsettle things.
  • Noise and too many people. A loud TV, dinner prep and visitors all at once.
  • Your own stress. People with dementia often pick up on tension around them.
  • Infections and medications. More on these below.

The Alzheimer's Association suggests keeping notes. For a week or two, jot down what happened in the hours before each rough evening: naps, meals, visitors, TV, pain, bathroom trips. Patterns often jump out.

What evening routine helps?

Predictability is calming. Try to keep waking, meals, activities and bedtime at about the same times every day. Then shape the afternoon to wind down.

  1. Front-load the day. Schedule doctor visits, bathing, outings and visitors for the morning or early afternoon, when the person is more alert.
  2. Plan something for the hard hour. If trouble starts around 4 p.m., have a calm activity ready at 3:30. Folding towels, sorting buttons, looking at old photos or a short walk can help burn off restlessness.
  3. Serve the bigger meal at lunch. The Alzheimer's Association suggests a lighter supper.
  4. Cut caffeine and alcohol later in the day. Mayo Clinic suggests keeping caffeine and sugar to the morning.
  5. Turn down the noise. Lower or switch off the TV news, keep visitors few and calm, and do loud chores earlier.
  6. Use soothing cues. Familiar music, nature sounds, a favorite movie, a hand massage or a warm drink without caffeine.
  7. Keep the bedtime ritual the same. Same order, same words, same time.

When agitation starts anyway

Stay calm and speak slowly. Ask if they need something: the bathroom, a snack, a sweater. Gently mention the time of day. Avoid arguing or correcting. Reassure them they are safe and you are there. If they need to pace, let them pace with supervision. The Alzheimer's Association advises against physical restraint.

And look after yourself. NIA suggests taking a few deep breaths or counting to 10 if you feel your own frustration rising.

How do light and sleep fit in?

Light is one of the strongest tools you have, and it is free.

  • Get daylight early. A morning walk, time on the porch or a chair by a sunny window helps set the body clock. In New Jersey's short winter days, this takes extra planning. Open every shade in the morning.
  • Turn lights on before dusk. Keep the home well lit as the sun goes down so shadows do not build. Close curtains once it is dark so windows do not turn into black mirrors.
  • Use night lights. Light the path from bed to bathroom. Mayo Clinic notes that night lights can ease agitation that comes with dark or unfamiliar surroundings.
  • Limit daytime naps. A short rest is fine. Long or late naps make nights worse.
  • Keep moving. Some physical activity every day helps sleep, but do not overschedule.
  • Watch evening fluids. The Alzheimer's Association suggests cutting back, not eliminating, drinks in the two hours before bed to reduce night bathroom trips.

Mayo Clinic says some research suggests a low dose of melatonin may help, alone or with bright daytime light. Ask the doctor before starting melatonin or any other supplement or sleep aid.

Fall-proofing matters at night too. See our fall prevention guide.

When should you call the doctor?

Call the doctor if sundowning starts suddenly, gets much worse in a few days, or comes with fever, pain, new incontinence or a change in eating. Mayo Clinic notes that a urinary tract infection or sleep apnea could be contributing, especially when symptoms come on quickly.

Bring a list of every medicine, including over-the-counter sleep aids, allergy pills and supplements. NIA notes that some medicines, or two medicines together, can cause agitation. Ask whether the timing of any dose could be changed.

Questions to ask:

  • Could an infection, pain, constipation or a sleep problem be behind this?
  • Could any of these medicines be making evenings worse?
  • Is there a better time of day to give them?
  • What should we try before medication, and what are the risks if we use one?

The Alzheimer's Association says most experts favor non-drug approaches first. When those are not enough, a doctor may prescribe medication for late-day agitation. Go over the risks and benefits together.

If the person becomes aggressive and anyone is in danger, call 911 and tell the dispatcher the person has dementia.

How do you keep someone safe in the evening?

Restlessness at dusk can turn into wandering. The Alzheimer's Association says six in 10 people living with dementia will wander at least once, and it can happen at any stage.

  • Plan for the risky hours. Activity and exercise at the time of day they tend to wander can reduce restlessness.
  • Secure the car keys. Someone who no longer drives may forget that. Wandering is not always on foot.
  • Secure doors. Door chimes, motion alerts or a lock placed high or low can buy you time.
  • Keep a recent photo on hand, along with medical information and a list of places they might try to go, such as a former home or job.
  • Use ID. An ID bracelet with your phone number helps responders.
  • Ask about Project Lifesaver. Several New Jersey county sheriffs, including Morris County, run this program, which uses a wristband transmitter to help find people who wander. Call your county sheriff's office to ask.
  • Tell the neighbors. A trusted neighbor who knows the situation can call you right away.

If your loved one goes missing, call 911 right away. Do not wait. Police can ask the New Jersey State Police to issue a Silver Alert for a missing person with dementia when the person is driving a known vehicle and is believed to be in danger.

Lock up kitchen knives, guns and dangerous tools as well, as NIA advises.

Where can New Jersey families get help?

You do not have to handle evenings alone. These are good first calls.

HelpPhoneNotes
Alzheimer's Association helpline1-800-272-390024 hours a day, 7 days a week. Ideal for a 2 a.m. call.
Alzheimer's New Jersey helpline1-888-280-6055Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m., translation in over 200 languages
Aging and Disability Resource Connection1-877-222-3737Your county office on aging: respite, JACC, adult day
Stress-Busting Program for Family Caregivers609-564-2617Nine-week small group class for dementia caregivers
Care2Caregivers peer support1-800-424-2494Rutgers peer counselors who have been family caregivers

Adult day. A good adult day program can make evenings easier, because the person has had a full, structured day and gets daylight and activity. The state's Alzheimer's Adult Day Services Program helps pay for adult day at participating centers, covering 20% to 100% of the cost for up to five days a week. You apply through the center. Program office: 609-438-4733.

Respite. If nights are wearing you down, the Statewide Respite Care Program and JACC can pay for in-home help or a short facility stay. Call the ADRC to start. Our respite guide has the 2026 limits, and our caregiver burnout guide has a one-week plan for getting relief.

For more, see our dementia support guide, ideas in activities for people with dementia, and, with the season coming, holidays with dementia. Our Find care help pages list care managers and adult day options.

faq.q: What time of day does sundowning start?
faq.a: It usually begins in the late afternoon or early evening, as daylight fades, and can last into the night. Many families notice a regular start time, which makes it easier to plan calm activities just before it begins.

faq.q: Can a UTI make sundowning worse?
faq.a: Yes. Mayo Clinic notes that a urinary tract infection or sleep apnea could be contributing to sundowning, especially when it comes on quickly. Call the doctor if behavior changes suddenly.

faq.q: Does melatonin help with sundowning?
faq.a: Mayo Clinic says some research suggests a low dose of melatonin may help, alone or with bright light during the day. Talk to the doctor before starting it or any other sleep aid.

faq.q: Who can I call at night about sundowning in New Jersey?
faq.a: The Alzheimer's Association helpline at 1-800-272-3900 answers 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. If anyone is in danger, call 911 and tell the dispatcher the person has dementia.

faq.q: Can adult day care help with sundowning?
faq.a: It often helps. A structured day with daylight, activity and company can make evenings calmer, and it gives the caregiver a break. New Jersey's Alzheimer's Adult Day Services Program helps pay for adult day at participating centers. Call the ADRC at 1-877-222-3737 for options in your county.
